newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lion shares surge on takeover rumours.
newsitem.headline: Lion shares surge on takeover rumours.

text.p: Shares in Australasian brewer Lion Nathan are being driven higher by rumours the company is a takeover target, analysts and stock brokers said on Friday.
The stock closed 12 cents stronger on Friday and has gained 32 cents in two weeks. At NZ$4.12, it is at its highest level since February, 1994.
Brokers said the market was buzzing with rumours that Lion was a the target of a corporate play, but there was little evidence to substantiate the view.
"I've heard noting that's not just whispers in the breeze," said Matthew Lynch at BZW. But he said he was sure there was something tangible behind the stock's rapid appreciation.
Analysts said the company's earnings outlook certainly didn't justify the rise in it's share price.
John Cairns, Lion analyst at Cavill White Securities, said he expected the company's 1996/97 profit to decline by about NZ$25-30 million on last year's $150.4 million.
"It certainly would be trading, just on straight earnings, at the top end of our fair value range," he said of the stock.
Lion Nathan spokesman Peter Hallwright said the company was unaware of anyone taking a substantial position in its stock.

Cairns agreed that there was little evidence to back up the takeover rumours, but he said it appeared someone with "reasonable fire power" was either taking a position or was buying stock in the belief somebody else would.
"If you look over the last quarter, the volumes that are going through on a rising price are pretty large. There have been some big parcels of stock going through," he said.

"It's not necessarily that anyone is actually building a stake. It could be that or, alternatively, there's someone out there who's taken a view that the company is in play or is likely to become a play."

Some brokers pointed out that Lion's market share in Australia had improved recently, and said the company also benefited from the weaker kiwi dollar, which has fallen against its Australian counterpart in recent weeks.
But analysts said neither reason justified the share's price gains. They said Lion's Australian market share had been in decline for the past three or four years.

"Over the last quarter or so it has picked up a few basis points, but the company does have some significent problems in its Australian market in terms of what's been happening to its market share over the past three or four years," said Cairns.

Nor, he said, was the New Zealand dollar's recent demise of any clear benefit, because Australian earnings were not physically converted back into Kiwi currency, just translated for reporting purposes.
"It's not as though all the earnings are remitted back into kiwi dollars, it's just at a point in time you're expressing those earnings in New Zealand currency," Cairns said.
Sean Vaughan at County Natwest said the takeover story was an old one which was trotted out every time the stock reached higher levels.
"I don't know of any legitimate stories with regard to corporate deals. The rumour is being bought at the moment -- we haven't seen the selling of the fact yet," he said.
But he agreed that the continued rise in Lion's share price was indicative of something more going on.
Whatever the case, brokers said investors were buying Lion shares with the expectation of some development.
"The share price is obviously anticipating some news," said BZW's Nigel Scott.
